pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in the Dordogne, founded 1115, whose celebrated relic of Christ's burial shroud was shown in 1934 to be a mediaeval Egyptian textile)
etymology: From the Perigord locality; the Occitan place name of the wooded valley in which the abbey was planted.
biblical_def: Cadouin was founded in 1115 in a wooded valley of the Périgord and affiliated to the Cistercians a few years later. Its fame rested almost entirely on a relic: a length of fine linen venerated for eight centuries as the cloth that bound Christ's head in the tomb. It drew pilgrims in great numbers, enriched the abbey, and was defended against periodic doubt. In 1934 the cloth's decorative bands were read as Kufic Arabic, and the textile was identified as Fatimid Egyptian work of the eleventh century — a thousand years too late and from the wrong religion. The entry is in this dictionary because the lesson is a biblical one. Scripture names a napkin in the tomb and then shows no interest in it whatever: “And the napkin, that was about his head, not lying with the linen clothes, but wrapped together in a place by itself” (Joh 20:7). Peter saw the linen and went away wondering about the resurrection, not the cloth: “he beheld the linen clothes laid by themselves, and departed, wondering in himself at that which was come to pass” (Luk 24:12). The grave clothes are evidence left behind, not a treasure to be kept.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines relic as the remains of a body after decay, and in the Romish church anything preserved as having belonged to a saint and reputed to possess miraculous power; shroud as a winding sheet for the dead; and counterfeit as made in imitation with a view to defraud.
webster_full: RELIC, n. That which remains; that which is left after the loss or decay of the rest; the remains of the body of a deceased person.
RELIC, n. In the Romish church, the remains of the body of a saint, or any thing which has belonged to a saint, preserved with great veneration as a sacred memorial.
SHROUD, n. The dress of the dead; a winding sheet; that in which a corpse is wrapped for burial.
COUNTERFEIT, a. Made in imitation of something, with a view to defraud by passing the false copy for genuine; forged; fictitious.
VENERATION, n. The highest degree of respect and reverence; respect mingled with some degree of awe.
scriptures: Joh 20:7
And the napkin, that was about his head, not lying with the linen clothes, but wrapped together in a place by itself.
Then arose Peter, and ran unto the sepulchre; and stooping down, he beheld the linen clothes laid by themselves, and departed, wondering in himself at that which was come to pass.
Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
corruption_summary: A Perigord abbey whose relic of Christ's burial cloth, venerated eight hundred years, proved in 1934 to be an eleventh-century Egyptian textile with Arabic inscriptions.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the relic trade entire, and Cadouin is its clearest single case because the exposure is documented. Scripture requires exactly the examination that was not made for eight centuries: “believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world” (1Jo 4:1), and the Bereans are commended for it — “and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11). A devotion that resents inspection has already told you what it is.

The deeper fault is not the forgery but the appetite that made forgery profitable. Faith that requires an object is not yet faith: “For we walk by faith, not by sight” (2Co 5:7), and Christ's own reproach was to men who would not believe without something to look at — “Except ye see signs and wonders, ye will not believe” (Joh 4:48). The principle to recover is a resurrection attested by witnesses and Scripture, needing no cloth at all.
roots_summary: Greek soudarion (G4676), a napkin; Greek sindon (G4616), fine linen; Greek dokimazo (G1381), to test; Hebrew sheqer (H8267), falsehood; Greek plane (G4106), error or delusion.
roots_lines: Greek soudarion (G4676) — a napkin or face cloth; “And the napkin, that was about his head” (Joh 20:7).
Greek sindon (G4616) — fine linen; the burial cloth of the gospels, mentioned and then dropped.
Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to test, to prove; “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1Th 5:21).
Hebrew sheqer (H8267) — falsehood, a lie; “for his molten image is falsehood, and there is no breath in them” (Jer 10:14).
Greek plane (G4106) — wandering, delusion; “God shall send them strong delusion, that they should believe a lie” (2Th 2:11).
usage: “wrapped together in a place by itself” (Joh 20:7) — all Scripture says of the cloth, and it is enough.
“try the spirits whether they are of God” (1Jo 4:1) — the examination eight centuries omitted.
“For we walk by faith, not by sight” (2Co 5:7) — the answer to the appetite relics feed.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in the Rouergue of south-west France, founded 1123 as a daughter of Pontigny; the name means the place of God)
etymology: Latin locus Dei, the place of God, through Occitan; the foundation charter is said to have renamed a wood formerly called the place of the devil.
biblical_def: Loc-Dieu was founded in 1123 in the Rouergue, a daughter of Pontigny, and its name is the entry's subject: locus Dei, the place of God, given to a site the local tradition had called the opposite. Fortified in the Hundred Years War and heavily restored in the nineteenth century, it survives as a private house with its church and chapter house intact. The naming instinct is thoroughly biblical, and the passage behind it is Jacob at Bethel: “And Jacob awaked out of his sleep, and he said, Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not” (Gen 28:16), and “How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven” (Gen 28:17). Jacob named a place because God had met him there, which is right. The error that grows out of it — and the medieval church fell into it everywhere — is to suppose the naming makes the place holy, so that the ground becomes a possession and the pilgrimage a necessity. Scripture locates the dwelling elsewhere: “Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations” (Psa 90:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines place as a particular portion of space of indefinite extent, and also a seat, residence or mansion; dwelling as a habitation, place of residence, abode; and consecrate as to set apart and devote to the service of God.
webster_full: PLACE, n. A particular portion of space of indefinite extent, occupied or capable of being occupied by any person or thing.
PLACE, n. A seat, residence, mansion; as, the gentleman has a place in the country.
DWELLING, n. Habitation; place of residence; abode.
CONSECRATE, v.t. To make or declare to be sacred, by certain ceremonies or rites; to appropriate to sacred uses; to devote to the service of God.
HOLY, a. Properly, whole, entire or perfect, in a moral sense; hence, pure in heart, temper or dispositions; also, hallowed; consecrated or set apart to a sacred use.
scriptures: And Jacob awaked out of his sleep, and he said, Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not.
And he was afraid, and said, How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.
Psa 90:1
A Prayer of Moses the man of God. Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations.
Joh 4:24
God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.
corruption_summary: A Rouergue abbey of 1123 named the place of God: naming a place for a meeting with God is Jacob's instinct, and supposing the name makes the ground holy is not.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's dwelling is not a location. “Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations” (Psa 90:1) reverses the expected direction — he is the dwelling, and the generations are the ones who move.

The live error is sacred geography, and it survives in Protestantism as the retreat centre and the favoured sanctuary where a man believes he can pray better. Christ answered the question directly when a woman raised it about mountains: “God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth” (Joh 4:24). The place of God, in the only sense that matters, is wherever a believer is.
roots_summary: Latin locus Dei, place of God; Hebrew maqom (H4725), a place; Hebrew Beth-el, house of God; Hebrew maon (H4583), a dwelling; Greek topos (G5117), a place.
roots_lines: Latin locus Dei — the place of God; the abbey's whole name and claim.
Hebrew maqom (H4725) — a place, a standing-place; “Surely the LORD is in this place” (Gen 28:16).
Hebrew Beth-el — house of God; “this is none other but the house of God” (Gen 28:17).
Hebrew maon (H4583) — a habitation; “thou hast been our dwelling place” (Psa 90:1).
Greek topos (G5117) — a place; in the New Testament never a holy site to be acquired.
usage: “and I knew it not” (Gen 28:16) — the place was holy by God's presence, not by Jacob's choosing.
“thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations” (Psa 90:1) — the dwelling is a person.
“must worship him in spirit and in truth” (Joh 4:24) — the end of the argument about places.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in the Aude of Languedoc, affiliated in the mid twelfth century; now a ruin in private hands)
etymology: Old French ville longue, the long settlement or farm, from Latin villa, a country estate, and longa, long.
biblical_def: Villelongue stands in the Aude, south-west of Carcassonne, a Cistercian house in the filiation of Bonnefont that grew from a small twelfth-century foundation into a modest abbey and then declined slowly through the wars of the later Middle Ages. Its church is roofless; what remains of the cloister and chapter house is in private hands. It is one of the many houses whose history is simply a long diminishment — no scandal, no suppression, no dramatic end, only centuries of fewer monks and smaller harvests until the buildings outnumbered the brethren. That ordinary trajectory deserves naming, because Scripture speaks a great deal about endurance and almost nothing about institutional survival. “For ye have need of patience, that, after ye have done the will of God, ye might receive the promise” (Heb 10:36) locates the promise beyond the doing; and the example offered is a man, not a foundation: “Ye have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the end of the Lord; that the Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy” (Jam 5:11). A house that shrank for four hundred years is not a failure in that light; it simply was never the thing that was promised to last.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines villa as a country seat or farm house, and in Italy a country residence; ruin as the remains of a decayed or demolished structure; and patience as the suffering of afflictions with a calm, unruffled temper.
webster_full: VILLA, n. A country seat or residence; originally, a farm or country house with its appendages.
RUIN, n. The remains of a decayed or demolished city, house or other work of men; destruction; fall; overthrow.
PATIENCE, n. The suffering of afflictions, pain, toil, calamity, provocation or other evil, with a calm, unruffled temper; endurance without murmuring or fretfulness.
DECLINE, v.i. To lean downward; to tend or draw toward a close; to fail; to sink; to decay.
ENDURE, v.i. To last; to continue in the same state without perishing; to remain; to abide.
scriptures: For ye have need of patience, that, after ye have done the will of God, ye might receive the promise.
Jam 5:11
Behold, we count them happy which endure. Ye have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the end of the Lord; that the Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy.
They shall perish, but thou shalt endure: yea, all of them shall wax old like a garment; as a vesture shalt thou change them, and they shall be changed:
But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved.
corruption_summary: A Languedoc Cistercian house whose history is a long diminishment: no scandal and no suppression, only four centuries of fewer monks.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that endurance is promised to persons and not to institutions. “But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved” (Mat 24:13) is singular; nothing in Scripture guarantees the continuance of a house, a denomination or a ministry.

The live comfort, and it is a real one, is that decline is not necessarily judgment. “They shall perish, but thou shalt endure: yea, all of them shall wax old like a garment” (Psa 102:26) treats the wearing out of made things as the ordinary order of creation. A congregation that is shrinking should ask whether it is faithful before it assumes it is cursed, and ask whether it is faithful before it assumes it is fine.
roots_summary: Latin villa longa, the long farm; Greek hupomone (G5281), patient endurance; Greek makrothumia (G3115), longsuffering; Hebrew qavah (H6960), to wait; Greek meno (G3306), to abide.
roots_lines: Latin villa longa — the long farm or settlement; a plain agricultural name, as Cistercian names usually are.
Greek hupomone (G5281) — endurance, a remaining under; “For ye have need of patience” (Heb 10:36).
Greek makrothumia (G3115) — longsuffering, long of temper; the companion virtue.
Greek meno (G3306) — to abide, remain; the verb of what lasts.
Hebrew qavah (H6960) — to wait, to look for with expectation; the Old Testament's patience.
usage: “that, after ye have done the will of God, ye might receive the promise” (Heb 10:36) — the promise is not the building.
“Behold, we count them happy which endure” (Jam 5:11) — said of persons.
“all of them shall wax old like a garment” (Psa 102:26) — the ordinary fate of made things.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in the Gers of Gascony, founded in the 1130s in the filiation of Morimond)
etymology: From the Gascon locality on the Gr ande Bais e; a local place name of uncertain derivation, probably from a stream or a green place.
biblical_def: Berdoues was founded in the 1130s in the valley of the Baïse in Gascony, in the Morimond line, and became the mother of further houses in the region, Gimont among them. Little of the abbey stands: the church was demolished after the Revolution and the site is partly a village and partly a garden. Its significance is as a mother house in a poor country — the Gascon abbeys were never rich, farmed thin land, and existed largely to settle and clear it. That makes Berdoues a good place to say something the romance of monasticism usually obscures: most of what these houses actually did was agriculture. The Cistercian granges drained, cleared, bred sheep and built mills, and they did it with lay brothers whose names nobody recorded. Scripture dignifies exactly that labour. “And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it” (Gen 2:15) puts work before the fall; “whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Col 3:23) sanctifies it without a vow; and “that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands” (1Th 4:11) is an apostolic command that describes a lay brother's day.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines agriculture as the cultivation of the ground for the purpose of producing vegetables and fruits for the use of man and beast; husbandry as the business of a farmer; and labor as exertion of muscular strength, toil, work.
webster_full: AGRICULTURE, n. In a general sense, the cultivation of the ground, for the purpose of producing vegetables and fruits for the use of man and beast.
HUSBANDRY, n. The business of a farmer, comprehending agriculture or tillage of the ground, the raising, managing and fattening of cattle and other domestic animals.
LABOR, n. Exertion of muscular strength, or bodily exertion which occasions weariness; particularly, the exertion of the limbs in occupations by which subsistence is obtained.
TILL, v.t. To labor; to cultivate; to plow and prepare for seed, and to dress crops.
GRANGE, n. A farm, with the buildings, stables, etc.; a farm house with the adjoining buildings.
scriptures: Gen 2:15
And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it.
Col 3:23
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;
And that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you;
In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury.
corruption_summary: A poor Gascon mother house of the 1130s, now mostly gone: a reminder that what these abbeys chiefly did was farm, with lay brothers whose names were never written down.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity of ordinary labour. “In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury” (Pro 14:23) is blunt about which of the two a household lives on, and the Cistercian granges were a better argument for the order than its treatises were.

The live corruption, treated more fully under Opus Dei, is the two tiers the system built: the choir monk who prayed and the lay brother who dug, with the first counted the higher calling. “whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Col 3:23) dissolves the ranking, and the men whose names were not recorded were doing God's work as fully as the men whose names were.
roots_summary: Hebrew abad (H5647), to work or serve; Hebrew adamah (H127), ground; Greek ergon (G2041), a work; Greek kopos (G2873), toil; Hebrew yagia (H3018), the labour of the hands.
roots_lines: Hebrew abad (H5647) — to work, till, serve; the same verb for farming and for worship.
Hebrew adamah (H127) — ground, soil; “to dress it and to keep it” (Gen 2:15).
Greek ergon (G2041) — a work or deed; the New Testament's common word for what a man does.
Greek kopos (G2873) — toil that wearies; “In all labour there is profit” (Pro 14:23) has the same realism.
Hebrew yagia (H3018) — toil, the produce of labour; what a grange actually yielded.
usage: “put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it” (Gen 2:15) — labour before the fall.
“and to work with your own hands” (1Th 4:11) — an apostolic command, not a lesser calling.
“In all labour there is profit” (Pro 14:23) — the economics of a Gascon grange.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in the Gers, a daughter of Berdoues, around which a bastide town was laid out in 1266)
etymology: From the Gascon locality; the abbey was first at Planselve and took the name of the bastide that grew beside it.
biblical_def: Gimont was a Cistercian house in the Gers, a daughter of Berdoues, and its interest lies in what happened around it: in 1266 a bastide — a planned new town on a grid, with a market hall and a charter of liberties — was laid out beside the abbey by agreement between the monks and the count of Toulouse. The town is still there, and its covered market still straddles the main street. A monastery that cooperated in founding a chartered town was doing something the Cistercian ideal of wilderness never anticipated, and it illustrates how thoroughly these houses became economic actors. Scripture is not against cities and does not share the romance of the wilderness. The exiles are told to invest in the city they are in: “And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace” (Jer 29:7). The end of the story is a city, not a desert: “For he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God” (Heb 11:10). A grid of streets and an honest market are nearer to that than a hermitage is.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines town as any collection of houses larger than a village; market as a public place in a town where provisions are exposed for sale; and charter as a written instrument executed with usual forms, given as evidence of a grant or contract.
webster_full: TOWN, n. Any collection of houses, larger than a village; also, in some states, a township; a civil division of territory.
MARKET, n. A public place in a city or town, where provisions or cattle are exposed for sale; also, the rate of purchase and sale.
CHARTER, n. A written instrument, executed with usual forms, given as evidence of a grant, contract or whatever is done between man and man.
LIBERTY, n. Freedom from restraint; also, privilege; exemption; immunity enjoyed by prescription or by grant.
FOUND, v.t. To lay the basis of any thing; to set, or place, as on something solid for support; to begin and build.
scriptures: Jer 29:7
And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.
For he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God.
By the blessing of the upright the city is exalted: but it is overthrown by the mouth of the wicked.
Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people.
corruption_summary: A Gascon Cistercian house beside which a chartered market town was laid out in 1266: an order founded for the wilderness helping to build a city.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that cities are a proper object of Christian labour and prayer. “By the blessing of the upright the city is exalted: but it is overthrown by the mouth of the wicked” (Pro 11:11) makes the righteous a civic asset, and “Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people” (Pro 14:34) says the same of a people.

The live tension is the one the Cistercians never resolved: an order constituted to flee the world became one of its most capable landlords and town-builders within a century and a half. That is not hypocrisy so much as the collapse of a false premise. “pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace” (Jer 29:7) was always the better instruction, and Gimont stumbled into it.
roots_summary: Hebrew ir (H5892), a city; Hebrew shalom (H7965), peace or welfare; Greek polis (G4172), a city; Greek themelios (G2310), a foundation; Hebrew tsedaqah (H6666), righteousness.
roots_lines: Hebrew ir (H5892) — a city; “seek the peace of the city” (Jer 29:7).
Hebrew shalom (H7965) — peace, wholeness, welfare; what the exiles were to seek for Babylon.
Greek polis (G4172) — a city; “a city which hath foundations” (Heb 11:10).
Greek themelios (G2310) — a foundation; the quality that distinguishes the promised city.
Hebrew tsedaqah (H6666) — righteousness; “Righteousness exalteth a nation” (Pro 14:34).
usage: “in the peace thereof shall ye have peace” (Jer 29:7) — the exiles told to invest in a city.
“whose builder and maker is God” (Heb 11:10) — the city that is the end of the story.
“By the blessing of the upright the city is exalted” (Pro 11:11) — the righteous as a civic good.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in the Rouergue of southern France, founded in the twelfth century; the name means the good valley)
etymology: French bonne combe, the good valley, from Latin bona, good, and a Gaulish word cumba, a hollow or small valley.
biblical_def: Bonnecombe was a Cistercian house in the Rouergue, founded in the twelfth century in a narrow wooded valley, and its name — the good valley — is as plain a specimen of Cistercian naming as exists. The order named its houses for water, light, valleys and clearings: Clairvaux the bright valley, Bonnecombe the good one, Clairefontaine the clear spring. The habit is worth noticing because Scripture's valleys are not pastoral but dangerous, and are good only because of who is in them. “Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me” (Psa 23:4) is the central text, and the comfort is in the final clause. “Who passing through the valley of Baca make it a well; the rain also filleth the pools” (Psa 84:6) makes a valley of weeping into a place of springs for those who pass through it toward God. The valley is a passage in Scripture and never an address, which is a gentle rebuke to an order that built its settlements in them and stayed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines combe as a hollow or valley between hills, chiefly in the south of England; valley as a hollow or low tract of land between hills; and good as valid, legally firm, and also sound, perfect, uncorrupted.
webster_full: COMBE, COOMB, n. A hollow, or valley between hills; a word found in many names of places.
VALLEY, n. A hollow or low tract of land between hills or mountains.
GOOD, a. Valid; legally firm; also, sound; perfect; uncorrupted; undamaged.
HOLLOW, n. A depression of surface; a cavity; a low place; a valley.
DALE, n. A low place between hills; a vale or valley.
scriptures: Psa 23:4
Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me.
Psa 84:6
Who passing through the valley of Baca make it a well; the rain also filleth the pools.
Isa 40:4
Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low: and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places plain:
For the LORD God is a sun and shield: the LORD will give grace and glory: no good thing will he withhold from them that walk uprightly.
corruption_summary: A Rouergue house in a narrow valley, named the good valley: Scripture's valleys are dangerous passages made good by who walks in them, not addresses.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the location of the comfort. “for thou art with me” (Psa 23:4) is why the valley of the shadow is survivable; nothing about the terrain is improved, and the Psalmist is walking through rather than settling.

The gentler point is about Cistercian naming itself, which is genuinely attractive and slightly misleading. A good valley, a bright valley, a clear spring — the names promise a found paradise, whereas Scripture's valleys are where weeping is turned into wells by those on the way somewhere: “Who passing through the valley of Baca make it a well” (Psa 84:6). The pilgrim makes the well; he does not find it.
roots_summary: Gaulish cumba, a hollow; Hebrew emeq (H6010), a valley; Hebrew gay (H1516), a ravine; Hebrew tsalmaveth (H6757), the shadow of death; Greek pharagx (G5327), a ravine.
roots_lines: Gaulish cumba — a hollow or small valley; the root of English combe and French combe.
Hebrew emeq (H6010) — a broad valley or plain between hills.
Hebrew gay (H1516) — a narrow ravine; “the valley of the shadow of death” (Psa 23:4).
Hebrew tsalmaveth (H6757) — deep shadow, the shadow of death; the darkness of that ravine.
Greek pharagx (G5327) — a ravine; “Every valley shall be exalted” (Isa 40:4) in its Greek form.
usage: “I will fear no evil: for thou art with me” (Psa 23:4) — what makes any valley good.
“the rain also filleth the pools” (Psa 84:6) — the pilgrim's valley, made a well by passing through.
“the LORD will give grace and glory” (Psa 84:11) — the destination that justifies the passage.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in the Chevreuse valley near Paris, founded 1118 and Cistercian from 1147; its buildings are now a luxury hotel)
etymology: French vaux, valleys, the plural of val, with the locality of Cernay; the valleys of Cernay.
biblical_def: Les Vaux-de-Cernay was founded in 1118 in a wooded valley of the Chevreuse south-west of Paris, affiliated to the Cistercians in 1147 through the Savigniac union, and became a substantial house under royal and noble patronage. Suppressed at the Revolution, the estate was bought in the nineteenth century by the Rothschild family, restored as a country property, and is now a luxury hotel and spa, with guests dining in the monastic ranges and the roofless church standing in the grounds. The irony needs no decoration from this dictionary; it needs the texts that bear on it. “That lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches, and eat the lambs out of the flock, and the calves out of the midst of the stall” (Amo 6:4) is Amos on comfortable religion; “There was a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day” (Luk 16:19) is the Lord's own portrait, and the parable ends badly. A cloister built to renounce comfort and now sold as comfort is a parable the building tells about itself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines luxury as a free indulgence in costly food, dress, furniture or any thing expensive which gratifies the appetites; sumptuous as costly, expensive, splendid; and ease as rest, an undisturbed state, freedom from pain or disturbance.
webster_full: LUXURY, n. A free or extravagant indulgence in the pleasures of the table; voluptuousness in the gratification of appetite; also, any thing delightful to the senses.
SUMPTUOUS, a. Costly; expensive; hence, splendid; magnificent; as a sumptuous house or table.
EASE, n. Rest; an undisturbed state; applied to the body, freedom from pain, disturbance, excitement or annoyance.
INDULGE, v.t. To gratify; to yield to the desire of; to give free course to, as the appetites or passions.
RENOUNCE, v.t. To disown; to disclaim; to reject; to cast off, as a right or title.
scriptures: Amo 6:4
That lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches, and eat the lambs out of the flock, and the calves out of the midst of the stall;
There was a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day:
Luk 6:24
But woe unto you that are rich! for ye have received your consolation.
Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy;
corruption_summary: A Chevreuse abbey of 1118, now a luxury hotel with guests in the monks' ranges: a cloister built to renounce comfort and sold as comfort.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption worth naming is not the hotel but the patronage that preceded it. A house under royal and noble favour was already drifting toward the thing it now sells, and Amos was written to exactly that condition: “That lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches” (Amo 6:4). The Lord's woe is equally direct: “But woe unto you that are rich! for ye have received your consolation” (Luk 6:24).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Paul's instruction to the comfortable, which is neither condemnation nor flattery: “Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy” (1Ti 6:17). The hotel's guests are not the villains of the entry; the drift that made the sale possible is.
roots_summary: French vaux, valleys; Hebrew shaanan (H7600), at ease; Greek truphe (G5172), luxury or indulgence; Greek paraklesis (G3874), consolation; Hebrew oneg (H6027), delight.
roots_lines: French vaux — valleys, plural of val; the house named for its hollows.
Hebrew shaanan (H7600) — secure, at ease, careless; Amos's word for the comfortable in Zion.
Greek truphe (G5172) — softness, luxury; used in the New Testament with disapproval.
Greek paraklesis (G3874) — consolation; “for ye have received your consolation” (Luk 6:24).
Hebrew oneg (H6027) — delight, exquisite pleasure; a good thing misdirected becomes Amos's target.
usage: “and fared sumptuously every day” (Luk 16:19) — the Lord's portrait of easy wealth.
“and eat the lambs out of the flock” (Amo 6:4) — comfort taken at the flock's expense.
“nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God” (1Ti 6:17) — the charge to the comfortable.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey north of Paris founded in 1228 by Louis IX; the royal mount)
etymology: French royal mont, the royal mount, from Latin regalis mons; named for its founder, the king.
biblical_def: Royaumont was founded in 1228 by the young Louis IX of France, who endowed it richly, worked on the building, and is said to have served the monks at table. It became the grandest Cistercian house in the Ile-de-France and the burial place of several of the royal family. Its church was quarried away after the Revolution; the ranges survive and the site is now a cultural foundation. The entry's subject is royal piety, which Scripture treats with great care and no sentimentality. A king may be genuinely devout and Scripture prays for it: “Give the king thy judgments, O God, and thy righteousness unto the king's son” (Psa 72:1). But the standard laid on a king is justice to the poor and not the endowment of monasteries, and the prophets judge kings on that: “He judged the cause of the poor and needy; then it was well with him: was not this to know me? saith the LORD” (Jer 22:16). Louis built abbeys and also led crusades and tightened the law against the Jews of France, and a dictionary that praised the first without naming the rest would be flattering a king, which is what court chroniclers are for.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines royal as kingly, pertaining to a king, becoming a king; patron as one who countenances, supports or protects; and endow as to furnish with a portion of estate, to settle a dower or permanent fund upon.
webster_full: ROYAL, a. Kingly; pertaining to a king; regal; as royal power or prerogative; also, becoming a king; magnificent.
PATRON, n. A protector; one who countenances or supports; in the church, one who has the gift and disposition of a benefice.
ENDOW, v.t. To furnish with a portion of estate; to settle a dower upon; also, to enrich with a permanent fund, as to endow a college.
MOUNT, n. A mass of earth, or earth and rock, rising considerably above the common surface of the surrounding land; a mountain; a hill.
JUSTICE, n. The virtue which consists in giving to every one what is his due; practical conformity to the laws and to principles of rectitude.
scriptures: Psa 72:1
A Psalm for Solomon. Give the king thy judgments, O God, and thy righteousness unto the king's son.
He judged the cause of the poor and needy; then it was well with him: was not this to know me? saith the LORD.
Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people.
Psa 72:4
He shall judge the poor of the people, he shall save the children of the needy, and shall break in pieces the oppressor.
corruption_summary: The grandest Cistercian house of the Ile-de-France, founded by Louis IX: royal piety that built abbeys, and a prophetic standard that asks about the poor instead.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the substitution of foundation for justice. A king who builds a monastery has done something visible; whether he has done the thing required is a separate question, and Jeremiah puts it to a king who preferred building: “He judged the cause of the poor and needy; then it was well with him: was not this to know me? saith the LORD” (Jer 22:16). The prayer for a king in Psalm 72 asks the same: “He shall judge the poor of the people, he shall save the children of the needy, and shall break in pieces the oppressor” (Psa 72:4).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that rulers are measured by righteousness and not by patronage. “Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people” (Pro 14:34) is the whole criterion, and it is as applicable to a modern government's religious gestures as to a thirteenth-century king's abbey.
roots_summary: Latin regalis mons, royal mount; Hebrew melek (H4428), a king; Hebrew mishpat (H4941), judgment; Hebrew tsedeq (H6664), righteousness; Greek basileus (G935), a king.
roots_lines: Latin regalis mons — the royal mount; a founder's name rather than a landscape's.
Hebrew melek (H4428) — a king; “Give the king thy judgments, O God” (Psa 72:1).
Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment, justice; the thing a king is for.
Hebrew tsedeq (H6664) — righteousness; the second half of the prayer for a king.
Greek basileus (G935) — a king; in the New Testament a figure to be prayed for and obeyed, never flattered.
usage: “was not this to know me? saith the LORD” (Jer 22:16) — justice to the poor as the test of a king's religion.
“he shall save the children of the needy” (Psa 72:4) — what is asked of a royal founder.
“but sin is a reproach to any people” (Pro 14:34) — the criterion no endowment satisfies.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in the Oise north of Paris, refounded in 1136 under royal patronage; now a museum and park)
etymology: From the locality of Chaalis in the forest of Ermenonville; a French place name of uncertain derivation.
biblical_def: Chaalis was refounded in 1136 in the forest of Ermenonville north of Paris, a daughter of Pontigny under the patronage of the French crown, and grew wealthy on royal favour and on the forest. Dismantled after the Revolution, the estate became a private domain and is now a museum and park in the care of a learned institute, with a ruined church, an intact chapel and a collection of art in the eighteenth-century abbot's lodging. That lodging is the heart of the entry: by the eighteenth century the commendatory abbots of Chaalis were building themselves a palace while the community dwindled. The arrangement is the abuse treated under commendam, here in its final and most visible form. Scripture's word for it is Ezekiel's: “Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?” (Eze 34:2). And the prophet is explicit about the mechanism: “Ye eat the fat, and ye clothe you with the wool, ye kill them that are fed: but ye feed not the flock” (Eze 34:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines commendatory as holding a benefice in commendam; lodging as a place of rest for the night, or a temporary habitation; and palace as a magnificent house in which an eminent person resides.
webster_full: COMMENDATORY, a. Holding a benefice in commendam; as a commendatory abbot or prior.
LODGING, n. A place of rest for the night, or a place of residence; a temporary habitation; apartments.
PALACE, n. A magnificent house in which an emperor, a king or other distinguished person resides; a splendid place of residence.
MUSEUM, n. A house or apartment appropriated as a repository of things that have an immediate relation to the arts.
DWINDLE, v.i. To diminish; to become less; to shrink; to waste or consume away.
scriptures: Eze 34:2

Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel, prophesy, and say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD unto the shepherds; Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?
Eze 34:3
Ye eat the fat, and ye clothe you with the wool, ye kill them that are fed: but ye feed not the flock.
But he that is an hireling, and not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth: and the wolf catcheth them, and scattereth the sheep.
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
corruption_summary: A royal Cistercian house whose commendatory abbots built themselves a palace while the community shrank: Ezekiel's shepherds who feed themselves, in stone.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is stated by the buildings. An abbot's eighteenth-century apartment, handsomely decorated, standing beside a church falling down and a handful of remaining monks, is “Ye eat the fat, and ye clothe you with the wool, ye kill them that are fed: but ye feed not the flock” (Eze 34:3) rendered as architecture. The Lord's own contrast applies: “But he that is an hireling, and not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not” (Joh 10:12).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Peter's charge, which forbids both the motive and the manner: “Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1Pe 5:2). The phrase among you is doing quiet work; an absentee cannot obey it.
roots_summary: Hebrew roeh (H7462), a shepherd; Hebrew tson (H6629), a flock; Greek poimaino (G4165), to tend a flock; Greek misthotos (G3411), a hireling; Greek episkopeo (G1983), to oversee.
roots_lines: Hebrew roeh (H7462) — a shepherd, one who feeds; “should not the shepherds feed the flocks?” (Eze 34:2).
Hebrew tson (H6629) — a flock of sheep or goats; the people, in the prophets.
Greek poimaino (G4165) — to tend as a shepherd; “Feed the flock of God which is among you” (1Pe 5:2).
Greek misthotos (G3411) — a hired man; “and not the shepherd” (Joh 10:12).
Greek episkopeo (G1983) — to oversee; the work an absentee abbot drew a salary for.
usage: “Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves!” (Eze 34:2) — the verdict the buildings illustrate.
“not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1Pe 5:2) — the motive required.
“whose own the sheep are not” (Joh 10:12) — why an absentee cannot be a pastor.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in the Aisne, founded 1131 as a daughter of Clairvaux; the long bridge)
etymology: French long pont, the long bridge, from Latin longus and pons; named for a causeway over the marshy ground of the site.
biblical_def: Longpont was founded in 1131 in the Aisne, a daughter of Clairvaux settled by Bernard himself, and grew into a large abbey with a Gothic church of cathedral scale. Sold at the Revolution and partly demolished, its great west front and the stumps of its nave still stand beside a surviving range, and the village keeps the name. That name — the long bridge — is the subject here, because a causeway over a marsh is exactly what a monastery was supposed not to need. Cistercian sites were chosen for their isolation and then made accessible by the monks' own engineering, since an abbey that cannot be reached cannot sell its wool or receive its guests. Scripture has little to say about bridges and a great deal about the way, and it is worth setting the two beside each other. “And an highway shall be there, and a way, and it shall be called The way of holiness” (Isa 35:8); “Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me” (Joh 14:6). The one road a man needs is a person, and no engineering is required of him to use it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bridge as any structure of wood, stone, brick or iron, raised over a river or other hollow place, for the passage of men and other animals; causeway as a way raised above the natural level by stones or earth; and way as a passage, that by which one passes.
webster_full: BRIDGE, n. Any structure of wood, stone, brick or iron, raised over a river, pond or lake, for the passage of men and other animals.
CAUSEWAY, n. A way raised above the natural level of the ground by stones, earth, timber, etc., serving as a dry passage over wet or marshy ground.
WAY, n. Literally, a passing; hence, a passage; the place of passing; a road; a highway; also, course; direction of motion.
HIGHWAY, n. A public road; a way open to all passengers; so called either because it is a great or public road, or because the earth was raised.
ACCESS, n. A coming to; near approach; admittance; admission; as to gain access to a prince.
scriptures: Isa 35:8

And an highway shall be there, and a way, and it shall be called The way of holiness; the unclean shall not pass over it; but it shall be for those: the wayfaring men, though fools, shall not err therein.
Joh 14:6
Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
Eph 2:18
For through him we both have access by one Spirit unto the Father.
By a new and living way, which he hath consecrated for us, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh;
corruption_summary: A Clairvaux daughter of 1131 named for the causeway that reached it: an order that chose unreachable sites and then built the roads to them.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that access to God needs no construction. “For through him we both have access by one Spirit unto the Father” (Eph 2:18) and “By a new and living way, which he hath consecrated for us, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh” (Heb 10:20) describe a road already laid, at a cost nobody else could pay.

The live irony is the Cistercian one. Remoteness was the point of the site and the first thing the monks had to overcome, and within a century the long bridge was carrying wool to market. “And an highway shall be there, and a way, and it shall be called The way of holiness” (Isa 35:8) promises a road into the kingdom; it does not promise one out to the fair.
roots_summary: Latin longus pons, long bridge; Hebrew derek (H1870), a way; Hebrew mesillah (H4546), a highway; Greek hodos (G3598), a way; Greek prosagoge (G4318), access.
roots_lines: Latin longus pons — the long bridge; a causeway over marsh, and the village's name still.
Hebrew derek (H1870) — a way, road, manner of life; the Old Testament's great moral metaphor.
Hebrew mesillah (H4546) — a raised highway; “And an highway shall be there” (Isa 35:8).
Greek hodos (G3598) — a way, road; “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (Joh 14:6).
Greek prosagoge (G4318) — access, introduction; “we both have access by one Spirit unto the Father” (Eph 2:18).
usage: “no man cometh unto the Father, but by me” (Joh 14:6) — the only causeway that matters.
“By a new and living way” (Heb 10:20) — a road already built, at a price.
“it shall be called The way of holiness” (Isa 35:8) — the highway promised to the redeemed.
